title: Nanocarriers & Targeted Delivery
summary: Understand how nanoscale carriers package drugs and steer them toward diseased tissue.

lessons.title: Liposomes and PEGylation

levels.kid:
Imagine blowing a soap bubble. Now imagine a bubble so tiny that hundreds of them could line up across one hair. Scientists can build bubbles like that out of fat. They are called **liposomes**.

A liposome has a watery middle where medicine can hide. Around it is a thin skin made of fat. The skin keeps the medicine inside until the bubble gets where it needs to go. That way, healthy parts of the body get less of the medicine.

But the body has cleaner cells called **macrophages**. They gobble up strange bubbles. So scientists gave the bubbles a fuzzy coat called **PEG**. It works like an invisibility cloak. The coated bubbles travel around much longer and have more time to reach sick spots, like tumors.
levels.hs:
A **liposome** is a tiny hollow sphere, usually around 50 to 200 nanometers across, made of the same kind of molecules that form cell membranes: **phospholipids**. Each phospholipid is **amphiphilic**, meaning it has a water-loving (hydrophilic) head and two water-fearing (hydrophobic) tails. In water, these molecules self-assemble into a **lipid bilayer**, tails tucked inside, that closes into a sphere around a watery core.

This structure gives two places to carry drugs:
- **Water-soluble drugs** sit in the aqueous core.
- **Fat-soluble drugs** dissolve in the bilayer itself.

British scientist **Alec Bangham** discovered liposomes in the 1960s while studying membranes.

The big early problem was that the immune system cleared plain liposomes within hours. Blood proteins stick to them and mark them for eating by macrophages of the **mononuclear phagocyte system**, especially **Kupffer cells** in the liver and macrophages in the spleen. The fix was **PEGylation**: attaching chains of **polyethylene glycol (PEG)** to the surface. PEG holds a layer of water that blocks proteins from sticking, so these **stealth liposomes** circulate for days instead of hours.

Real example: **Doxil**, approved in the US in 1995, packages the cancer drug doxorubicin in PEGylated liposomes. It causes much less heart damage than free doxorubicin, though it can cause a skin reaction on the palms and soles called hand-foot syndrome.
levels.college:
**Composition.** Most pharmaceutical liposomes combine a phosphatidylcholine (such as hydrogenated soy PC, HSPC, or DSPC) with **cholesterol**. Cholesterol fills gaps between acyl chains, tightening the bilayer and reducing drug leakage. Lipids with saturated chains have a high **phase transition temperature (Tm)**: DSPC melts from a rigid gel to a fluid state near 55 °C, so at body temperature its bilayer stays gel-like and leaks little.

**Size and lamellarity.** Liposomes are classed as small unilamellar (SUV, under ~100 nm), large unilamellar (LUV, ~100 nm to 1 µm) or multilamellar (MLV, onion-like layers). Bangham's **thin-film hydration** (dry the lipid film, add water) gives MLVs; **extrusion** through polycarbonate membranes then produces uniform LUVs.

**Loading.**
- *Passive*: drug is trapped during formation; efficiency is often low.
- *Remote (active) loading*: an **ammonium sulfate gradient** pulls weak bases like doxorubicin into the core, where they become trapped. Efficiencies exceed 90%.

**Why PEG works.** Plain liposomes adsorb **opsonins** (complement proteins, immunoglobulins), which trigger uptake by liver and spleen macrophages. Grafting about 5 mol% of **mPEG2000-DSPE** (PEG anchored to a lipid) creates a hydrated, flexible steric barrier that reduces opsonin binding. Doxil's circulation half-life in humans is roughly 2 to 3 days, versus minutes for free doxorubicin's distribution phase.

**Drawbacks.** Repeat dosing can provoke **anti-PEG IgM** antibodies, causing the **accelerated blood clearance (ABC)** phenomenon, in which a later dose is removed rapidly. PEG also hinders uptake by target cells.

**Approved examples:**
- **Doxil/Caelyx** (PEGylated doxorubicin; ovarian cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, myeloma)
- **AmBisome** (non-PEGylated amphotericin B; far less kidney toxicity)
- **Onivyde** (PEGylated irinotecan; pancreatic cancer)
- **Vyxeos** (daunorubicin plus cytarabine; acute myeloid leukemia)
levels.phd:
**Origins of stealth.** Before PEG, Allen and Chonn (1987) prolonged circulation by incorporating ganglioside GM1. In 1990, Klibanov, Maruyama, Torchilin and Huang, alongside the Papahadjopoulos and Lasic/Woodle groups, showed that PEG-lipid conjugates were more effective, cheaper and more reproducible. Doxil's bilayer is roughly HSPC:cholesterol:mPEG2000-DSPE at a 56:38:5 molar ratio, at about 80 to 100 nm.

**Polymer physics of the PEG layer.** A grafted PEG chain occupies a region set by its Flory radius, R_F ≈ aN^(3/5), about 3.5 nm for PEG2000. When the distance between graft sites (D) exceeds R_F, chains adopt a **mushroom** conformation with exposed gaps. When D < R_F, neighbouring chains crowd and extend into a **brush**, giving denser steric protection. Around 5 mol% PEG2000 sits in the brush regime. Above roughly 7 to 10 mol%, PEG-lipids begin to form micelles and destabilize the bilayer.

**Remote loading chemistry.** In Barenholz's ammonium sulfate method, neutral NH3 escapes the liposome, leaving protons behind and acidifying the core. Uncharged doxorubicin diffuses in, becomes protonated and membrane-impermeant, then precipitates with sulfate as fibrous bundles seen on cryo-TEM. This intraliposomal gel keeps leakage in plasma very low.

**The release paradox.** Stability is a double-edged sword. SPI-077, a stealth liposomal cisplatin, reached tumors well but released so little drug that it showed minimal activity. Encapsulated drug is not bioavailable drug; therapeutic effect depends on release kinetics at the target.

**Pharmacokinetics and outcomes.** PEGylated liposomes behave as a near-plasma-volume reservoir with markedly reduced clearance. The O'Brien et al. (2004) phase III trial in metastatic breast cancer found PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin comparable to conventional doxorubicin for progression-free survival, with significantly less cardiotoxicity. Lower peak free-drug levels and reduced delivery to myocardium, whose continuous capillaries exclude ~100 nm particles, likely explain the benefit. The safety gain was larger than any efficacy gain.

**The PEG dilemma.** The same layer that blocks opsonins also blocks binding to target cells and endosomal escape. This motivated **sheddable PEG**, built on linkers that cleave under acidic pH or reducing conditions.
levels.expert:
**Immunology of PEG in practice.** The ABC phenomenon, characterized by Ishida and Kiwada, is driven by splenic marginal zone B cells that make anti-PEG IgM in a largely T-cell-independent response. On re-exposure, IgM fixes complement and opsonizes the carrier. Notably, ABC is weaker with Doxil than with empty PEGylated liposomes, probably because doxorubicin is toxic to the responding B cells. Separately, **pre-existing anti-PEG antibodies** are common, likely from PEG in cosmetics and laxatives; some assays detect them in a majority of contemporary samples. The REG1 anticoagulant trial (pegnivacogin) was halted for severe allergic reactions linked to these antibodies.

**Infusion reactions.** Szebeni described **complement activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA)**: acute flushing, chest tightness and blood pressure changes during first infusions, without prior sensitization. Standard mitigation is a slower initial infusion rate and premedication per protocol.

**Product successes and failures.**
- **Vyxeos** (CPX-351) co-encapsulates daunorubicin and cytarabine at a fixed synergistic 1:5 molar ratio. It improved overall survival in older patients with secondary AML (Lancet et al., 2018), showing that liposomes can control drug ratios, not just distribution.
- **ThermoDox**, a heat-triggered lyso-thermosensitive liposome, missed its primary endpoint in the phase III HEAT trial in liver cancer, a cautionary tale about triggered release in heterogeneous tumors.

**Generics and quality.** The 2011 to 2013 Doxil shortage exposed how hard liposomes are to copy. The FDA's 2018 liposome guidance and product-specific guidances require matching lipid composition, size distribution, lamellarity, internal pH and drug state, and in vitro release, plus separate bioequivalence for free and encapsulated drug. A common analytical pitfall is reporting only total plasma drug, which overstates what is pharmacologically available.

**Open questions.**
- Which PEG replacements will win: polysarcosine, poly(2-oxazoline) or zwitterionic polycarboxybetaine?
- Can imaging select patients? Ferumoxytol MRI predicted lesion uptake of liposomal irinotecan in an early study.
- For brain tumors, can direct infusion bypass the blood-brain barrier? Convection-enhanced delivery of rhenium-186 nanoliposomes into glioblastoma is under clinical study.

keyPoints: Liposomes are phospholipid bilayer vesicles with an aqueous core
Water-soluble drugs go in the core, fat-soluble drugs in the bilayer
Cholesterol and high-Tm saturated lipids reduce drug leakage
PEGylation creates a stealth coat that slows uptake by liver and spleen macrophages
Doxil (1995) cut doxorubicin heart toxicity; drug release still governs efficacy
Anti-PEG antibodies can cause accelerated blood clearance and infusion reactions

Its bilayer was too fluid and leaked during circulation

choices: Lowering PEG-lipid content so grafts sit farther apart
Adding more cholesterol to rigidify the lipid bilayer
Swapping saturated DSPC for an unsaturated, low-Tm lipid
Raising PEG-lipid density so graft spacing falls below R_F

Doxorubicin is protonated in the acidic core and precipitates

advancedTest.q: A patient's second PEGylated liposome infusion clears far faster than the first. Which mechanism best fits?

Hepatic enzymes induced by the first dose degrade the lipids
First-dose CARPA permanently depleted complement proteins
Kupffer cells shrank after saturation and now take up less
advancedTest.explain: This is the ABC phenomenon. Marginal zone B cells produce anti-PEG IgM, which opsonizes the next dose through complement. Depleted complement or fewer Kupffer cells would slow clearance, not speed it.

lessons.title: Lipid Nanoparticles for mRNA and siRNA

levels.kid:
Imagine you want to send a tiny recipe card into a cell so it can build a helpful protein, like a piece of a vaccine. The recipe card is called mRNA, but it's very fragile and cells don't let strangers in easily.

Scientists wrap the recipe card in a tiny fatty bubble called a **lipid nanoparticle**, like bubble wrap made of fat. The bubble floats to a cell, gets pulled inside, and then pops open so the recipe card can get to work.

This bubble trick is how COVID-19 mRNA vaccines protect people, and how similar bubbles carry tiny silencer molecules called siRNA to calm down a harmful liver gene that causes nerve damage elsewhere in the body.
levels.hs:
A **lipid nanoparticle (LNP)** is a tiny fat-based capsule, usually 80-150 nanometers wide, built to protect and deliver fragile nucleic acids like **mRNA** or **siRNA** into cells. Naked RNA is quickly destroyed by enzymes in blood and can't cross cell membranes on its own, so it needs a vehicle.

An LNP is built from four ingredients:
- An **ionizable lipid**, the key component. It's neutral at the blood's pH (7.4), which keeps the particle gentle on tissues, and gains a positive charge in the mildly acidic conditions used during manufacturing so it can grab onto the RNA.
- **Cholesterol**, which fills gaps and stabilizes the structure.
- A **phospholipid**, which helps form the particle's outer layer.
- A small amount of **PEG-lipid**, which forms a protective surface coating and controls particle size.

Once inside a cell's endosome (an acidic internal pocket), the ionizable lipid becomes positively charged again, which disrupts the endosome's membrane and releases the RNA into the cytoplasm so it can act.

This technology is best known for the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna **COVID-19 mRNA vaccines**, and it also delivers **patisiran**, an siRNA drug that quiets a liver gene causing a hereditary nerve disease.
levels.college:
Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are self-assembling, non-liposomal fat particles engineered to encapsulate and deliver nucleic acid therapeutics such as mRNA and small interfering RNA (siRNA). Four lipid components work together:

- **Ionizable lipid** (e.g., DLin-MC3-DMA in patisiran; SM-102 and ALC-0315 in mRNA vaccines): carries an apparent pKa near 6.2-6.5. During formulation at low pH it is protonated and electrostatically complexes the negatively charged RNA phosphate backbone; at physiological blood pH it returns to a near-neutral state, lowering toxicity and immune recognition during circulation.
- **Cholesterol**: intercalates between lipid chains, increasing membrane rigidity and particle stability.
- **Helper phospholipid** (commonly DSPC): supports bilayer-like packing at the particle surface.
- **PEG-lipid**: forms a hydrophilic outer shell that controls particle size, limits aggregation, and slows protein adsorption.

**Manufacturing** uses rapid microfluidic mixing: an ethanol phase containing the lipids is combined with an acidic aqueous phase containing the RNA. The abrupt solvent shift drives nanoprecipitation and self-assembly, after which dialysis or tangential-flow filtration removes ethanol and raises the pH to neutral, settling the ionizable lipid's surface charge near zero.

**Cellular uptake and escape**: After intravenous injection, particles are coated with plasma proteins, especially **apolipoprotein E**, which guides them to hepatocytes via the LDL receptor, explaining the liver's dominance as a default target organ. Cells internalize LNPs by endocytosis. Inside the acidifying endosome, the ionizable lipid becomes cationic, interacts with anionic endosomal membrane lipids, and promotes formation of non-bilayer structures that destabilize the membrane, letting a small fraction of RNA escape into the cytosol where it can be translated (mRNA) or loaded into the RNA-induced silencing complex (siRNA).
levels.phd:
The ionizable lipid is the functional heart of an LNP, and its structure-activity relationship was defined largely through combinatorial libraries screened by Jayaraman and colleagues in 2012, which identified DLin-MC3-DMA as the first clinical-grade ionizable lipid, later used in patisiran (Onpattro, approved 2018 for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis). Newer generations, SM-102 (Spikevax) and ALC-0315 (Comirnaty), feature branched tails and ester or amide linkages tuned for an apparent pKa of roughly 6.2-6.5, balancing RNA complexation, endosomal escape, and systemic tolerability.

Mechanistically, at endosomal pH (around 5 to 6.5) the protonated ionizable lipid forms ion pairs with anionic endosomal phospholipids such as phosphatidylserine, generating a cone-shaped lipid geometry that favors transition from a bilayer (lamellar) to an inverted hexagonal or cubic phase. This non-bilayer transition destabilizes the endosomal membrane and permits RNA release into the cytosol. Despite this, single-molecule imaging by Gilleron and colleagues in 2013 showed that roughly 1-2% of internalized siRNA escapes productively, identifying endosomal escape, rather than cellular uptake, as the major efficiency bottleneck for RNA nanomedicines.

LNP composition also dictates biodistribution independent of active targeting. Surface-adsorbed apolipoprotein E drives hepatocyte-selective uptake via the LDL receptor and LRP1, which is why nearly all approved LNP therapeutics are liver-directed. Charge ratio (N/P, the molar ratio of ionizable amine to RNA phosphate, typically 3 to 6) and PEG-lipid identity or density modulate particle size, serum protein adsorption, and circulation half-life; PEG shedding kinetics are tuned via the PEG-lipid's acyl chain length (C14 versus C18), trading stealth against efficient cellular uptake.

A notable controversy concerns anti-PEG antibodies, present in a meaningful fraction of the population from prior exposure to PEGylated consumer products, which can accelerate blood clearance of subsequent LNP doses, relevant to repeat-dose mRNA vaccination and RNA therapeutics alike.
levels.expert:
Clinically, LNPs are expanding beyond the liver. Siegwart and colleagues demonstrated Selective Organ Targeting (SORT): adding a fifth, permanently charged lipid (cationic or anionic) to the canonical four-component formulation shifts biodistribution from liver toward lung or spleen in a manner that tracks with overall particle surface charge and the protein corona it attracts, without a targeting ligand. This has opened routes toward inhaled or intravenous mRNA delivery to pulmonary epithelium and splenic immune cells, including for in vivo CAR-T cell programming and cancer immunotherapy.

A second frontier is in vivo gene editing: Intellia's NTLA-2001 uses an LNP built on an ionizable lipid related to MC3 to co-deliver Cas9 mRNA and a guide RNA systemically to hepatocytes, achieving durable knockdown of serum transthyretin after a single infusion in patients with transthyretin amyloidosis, showing LNPs can deliver editing machinery, not just antisense or interference payloads.

LNPs are not immunologically inert carriers. Independent of the RNA cargo, the particles themselves can act as adjuvants: ionizable lipids and residual double-stranded RNA byproducts of in vitro transcription can trigger innate sensors such as TLR4, TLR7/8, RIG-I, and inflammasome pathways, contributing to the reactogenicity seen after mRNA vaccination. Nucleoside modification of mRNA with N1-methylpseudouridine, building on Karikó and Weissman's work, dampens RNA-intrinsic innate activation but does not remove LNP-intrinsic signaling.

Manufacturing quality control remains a practical bottleneck at scale: batch consistency depends on precise control of microfluidic mixing rates (staggered-herringbone or T-junction mixers), encapsulation efficiency assayed via dye-exclusion assays, particle size and polydispersity measured by dynamic light scattering, and residual solvent levels, all now codified in regulatory guidance for RNA-LNP products. Cryo-electron microscopy reveals that mRNA-LNPs often have an amorphous, multi-compartment internal structure rather than the single electron-dense core typical of siRNA-LNPs, a difference linked to mRNA's larger size and the kinetics of microfluidic mixing.

keyPoints: LNPs assemble from four lipids: ionizable lipid, cholesterol, phospholipid, and PEG-lipid
The ionizable lipid is neutral at blood pH but becomes charged in the acidic endosome
Endosomal escape, not cellular uptake, is the main efficiency bottleneck for RNA delivery
Apolipoprotein E adsorption drives default LNP targeting to liver hepatocytes
Patisiran (siRNA) and Comirnaty/Spikevax (mRNA) are approved LNP-based drugs
SORT lipids and in vivo gene editing are extending LNPs beyond the liver

lessons.title: Polymeric Nanoparticles, Micelles and Dendrimers

levels.kid:
Some medicines are like shy travelers. They do not mix with water, and blood is mostly water. So scientists build tiny carriers to give them a ride. These carriers are so small that hundreds could line up across the width of one hair.

- **Polymer nanoparticles** are tiny balls made of a plastic-like material that the body slowly breaks apart, a bit like a sugar cube melting in tea. As the ball breaks apart, medicine leaks out little by little.
- **Micelles** are balls with an oily middle and a watery outside. The oily medicine hides in the middle, safe from the water.
- **Dendrimers** look like tiny bushy trees. Medicine can tuck inside the branches or hang on the tips.

Each carrier helps a medicine travel safely to where it is needed.
levels.hs:
A **nanoparticle** is a particle measured in nanometers (billionths of a meter). Medical nanoparticles are usually about 10 to 200 nm across, far smaller than a red blood cell (about 7,000 nm). This lesson covers three carriers built from **polymers**, which are long chains of repeating units.

- **Polymeric nanoparticles** are solid spheres made from polymers. The most popular is **PLGA**, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid). Water slowly breaks its bonds, turning it into lactic acid and glycolic acid, which the body handles naturally. As the particle breaks down, the drug is released gradually.
- **Polymeric micelles** form from **amphiphilic** polymers: one end loves water, the other avoids it. In water, many chains cluster so the water-avoiding ends hide in a core and the water-loving ends form a shell. Fat-soluble drugs sit in the core. Micelles assemble only above a threshold called the **critical micelle concentration (CMC)**.
- **Dendrimers** are tree-like molecules built outward in layers called **generations**. Each new generation roughly doubles the number of branch tips.

Real example: the cancer drug **paclitaxel** barely dissolves in water. The original product, Taxol, used a castor-oil solvent called Cremophor EL that can trigger serious allergic reactions. **Genexol-PM** packs paclitaxel into polymer micelles instead, removing the need for that solvent. It was approved in South Korea in 2007.
levels.college:
**Polymeric nanoparticles** come in two architectures. **Nanospheres** are matrix systems with drug dispersed throughout a solid polymer; **nanocapsules** have a drug-containing core (oily or aqueous) surrounded by a polymer shell. Common polymers include PLGA, PLA, polycaprolactone (PCL), chitosan and, for protein-based carriers, albumin.

Preparation methods:
- **Nanoprecipitation** (solvent displacement): polymer and hydrophobic drug dissolved in a water-miscible solvent such as acetone are added to water; the polymer precipitates into particles.
- **Single emulsion (o/w)**: suitable for hydrophobic drugs; the organic solvent is then evaporated.
- **Double emulsion (w/o/w)**: used to trap water-soluble cargo such as proteins.

Release is typically **biphasic**: an initial **burst** from drug near the surface, then slower release by **diffusion** and polymer **erosion**. PLGA degradation is tunable. A 50:50 lactide:glycolide ratio degrades fastest (weeks), while lactide-rich grades such as 75:25 degrade more slowly because lactide's methyl group makes the polymer more hydrophobic. Higher molecular weight also slows degradation.

**Polymeric micelles** form from block copolymers such as PEG-b-PLA, PEG-b-PCL or Pluronics (PEO-PPO-PEO). They are typically 10 to 100 nm across. The hydrophobic core solubilizes the drug, and the PEG corona provides steric stability. Drugs can be physically entrapped or chemically conjugated to the core-forming block. Charged blocks can form **polyion complex micelles** with oppositely charged cargo such as nucleic acids.

**Dendrimers** consist of a core, repeating branching units and terminal surface groups. The classic is **PAMAM** (poly(amidoamine)). With an ethylenediamine core, surface groups double per generation: 4 at G0, 8 at G1, 16 at G2, up to 64 at G4. Drugs can be:
- encapsulated in interior cavities,
- bound electrostatically,
- covalently attached to surface groups.

Amine-terminated (cationic) PAMAM is cytotoxic and hemolytic because positive charges disrupt cell membranes, so surfaces are often modified with hydroxyl, acetyl, carboxyl or PEG groups.
levels.phd:
**PLGA erosion kinetics.** PLGA undergoes **bulk erosion**: water penetrates faster than ester hydrolysis proceeds, so chains cleave throughout the matrix. Carboxylic acid end groups catalyze further hydrolysis (**autocatalysis**), and because acidic oligomers diffuse out slowly, larger particles and devices can develop an acidic interior microclimate, reported to reach pH 2 to 3 in microspheres. Counterintuitively, larger particles can therefore degrade faster in their centers. The acidic interior can also denature encapsulated proteins. By contrast, **polyanhydrides** hydrolyze so quickly that they erode from the surface inward (**surface erosion**), giving closer-to-zero-order release.

**Micelle thermodynamics versus kinetics.** Block copolymer micelles have CMCs often in the micromolar range or lower, orders of magnitude below small-molecule surfactants (often millimolar). They also show **kinetic stability**: a glassy (PLA, with a glass transition above body temperature) or entangled core slows unimer exchange, so micelles can persist transiently below the CMC. However, buffer-based stability overestimates in vivo behavior. Chen and colleagues (2008) used in vivo FRET imaging with dye-loaded PEG-PDLLA micelles and found cargo release within roughly 15 minutes of intravenous injection. Lipoproteins, albumin and cell membranes act as sinks that extract lipophilic cargo. Strategies to improve retention include **core crosslinking** (e.g., CriPec technology, in which docetaxel is linked through a hydrolyzable linker into a crosslinked core, as in CPC634), drug-polymer conjugation, and π-π stacking or hydrogen bonding in the core.

**Dendrimer synthesis and size.** Tomalia's group at Dow reported PAMAM "starburst" dendrimers in 1985 using **divergent** synthesis, growing outward from the core. Hawker and Fréchet introduced **convergent** synthesis in 1990, building dendrons first and attaching them to a core, which gives fewer defects but caps the achievable size. PAMAM diameter grows about 1 nm per generation: G4 is about 4.5 nm, G5 about 5.4 nm and G7 about 8 nm. Because the glomerular filtration cutoff is roughly 5 to 6 nm, low-generation, neutral dendrimers are cleared renally while larger ones circulate longer. At high generations (around G10 for PAMAM), steric crowding at the surface (de Gennes dense packing) limits ideal growth. Toxicity scales with generation and cationic charge density; neutral (hydroxyl) and anionic (carboxyl) surfaces are far better tolerated.
levels.expert:
**Clinical track record.** Polymer nanocarriers have produced few approvals relative to effort. Genexol-PM (paclitaxel in PEG-PDLLA micelles) is approved in South Korea and some other countries. Apealea (paclitaxel in a retinoid-based micellar system) gained EU approval in 2018 for ovarian cancer, although its marketing authorisation was later withdrawn. NK105, a PEG-polyaspartate paclitaxel micelle from Kataoka's platform, missed its phase 3 progression-free survival noninferiority endpoint versus paclitaxel in breast cancer. BIND-014, a PSMA-targeted PEG-PLGA docetaxel particle, showed modest phase 2 activity, and BIND Therapeutics went bankrupt in 2016. CRLX101, a cyclodextrin-polymer camptothecin conjugate, was discontinued. Dendrimers reached patients through astodrimer sodium (SPL7013, a polylysine dendrimer with naphthalene disulfonate surface groups), marketed as VivaGel BV for bacterial vaginosis in Australia and Europe, and OP-101, a hydroxyl PAMAM-N-acetylcysteine conjugate tested in severe COVID-19. OP-101 builds on Kannan and colleagues' 2012 work showing hydroxyl PAMAM accumulates in activated microglia. The neurosurgical cousin is Gliadel, a surface-eroding polyanhydride wafer releasing carmustine into the resection cavity after glioma surgery: a macroscale implant using the same erosion chemistry.

**Development pitfalls:**
- **Misleading release assays.** Dialysis in sink buffer rarely predicts in vivo leakage; biorelevant media containing albumin or lipoproteins are more informative.
- **Total versus encapsulated drug.** Plasma pharmacokinetics that report total drug can mask premature release. Assays separating carrier-bound from released drug are needed.
- **Low loading.** PLGA particles often carry under 10% drug by weight, so more polymer is needed to carry a given amount of drug.
- **Sterilization.** PLGA tolerates neither autoclaving nor gamma irradiation well (molecular weight drops); 0.22 µm sterile filtration constrains particle size, pushing toward aseptic manufacture.
- **Lyophilization** requires cryoprotectants such as trehalose or sucrose to prevent aggregation.
- **Batch variability.** PLGA end-capping, molecular weight distribution and supplier differences alter release. Commercial PAMAM above about G5 contains structural defects, so it is less monodisperse than often claimed.

**Advances and open questions.** Microfluidic mixing and flash nanoprecipitation (Johnson and Prud'homme) give tighter size control and scalability. The FDA's 2022 guidance on drug products containing nanomaterials sets characterization expectations. Unresolved issues include predicting in vivo carrier integrity and justifying added complexity over simpler formulations.

PLGA degrades by ester hydrolysis; 50:50 grades degrade fastest
Release is usually biphasic: initial burst, then diffusion and erosion
Block copolymer micelles self-assemble above the CMC with a drug-loaded hydrophobic core
Dendrimers are branched polymers built in generations; surface groups double each generation
Cationic dendrimer surfaces are toxic; hydroxyl, carboxyl or PEG surfaces are safer

test.explain: The 50:50 ratio degrades fastest. Lactide-rich grades are more hydrophobic because of lactide's methyl group, so they hydrolyze more slowly.

test.explain: Below the critical micelle concentration (CMC), the polymer chains stay as separate unimers instead of clustering.

kidTest.explain: They give medicines that do not mix with water a safe ride through the blood.

kidTest.explain: A micelle has an oily middle, so oily medicine hides there, away from water.

kidTest.explain: Dendrimers branch out again and again, like a bushy tree.

kidTest.explain: Micelles keep oily medicine in their middle and water-loving parts on the outside.

advancedTest.q: In vivo FRET imaging showed PEG-PDLLA micelles losing their cargo within about 15 minutes of injection, despite good stability in buffer. The best interpretation is:
choices: Micelles are cleared by the kidney before they assemble
The PEG corona triggers drug crystallization in the core
Blood components extract cargo faster than buffer tests show
FRET signal mainly reflects dye binding to red cells
advancedTest.explain: Lipoproteins, albumin and membranes act as sinks that pull lipophilic cargo out of micelles. Simple buffer release tests therefore overestimate in vivo retention.

advancedTest.q: Larger PLGA particles can degrade faster in their centers than smaller ones. Why?
choices: Esterases penetrate large particles more easily than small
Larger particles absorb more light and heat up internally
Acidic breakdown products build up and catalyze hydrolysis
Surface erosion is faster when surface area is smaller
advancedTest.explain: Carboxylic acid oligomers diffuse out slowly from large particles, so an acidic microclimate forms and autocatalyzes ester hydrolysis. PLGA erodes in bulk, not mainly from the surface.

advancedTest.q: A team wants a PAMAM dendrimer with low membrane toxicity that can still be cleared by the kidneys. Which is the best choice?
advancedTest.explain: G4 is about 4.5 nm, under the roughly 5 to 6 nm renal cutoff, and its neutral hydroxyl surface is well tolerated. G2 amine is small but cationic and toxic; G8 carboxyl is tolerated but too large for renal clearance.

advancedTest.q: Why can a block copolymer micelle persist briefly below its CMC, unlike a small-surfactant micelle?
choices: Its glassy or entangled core slows chain exchange
Its PEG shell covalently bonds to plasma proteins
Its cargo raises the osmotic pressure of the blood
Its CMC rises sharply as it is diluted
advancedTest.explain: Polymeric micelles are kinetically stable: a glassy or entangled core slows unimer exchange, so disassembly lags behind dilution. Thermodynamics alone would predict breakup below the CMC.

lessons.title: The EPR Effect and Active Targeting Ligands

levels.kid:
Imagine a city where the roads are pipes full of moving water. Healthy pipes are sealed tight, so big boats stay inside. But near a tumor, the pipes are built in a hurry. They have cracks and gaps!

Tiny medicine bubbles, called **nanoparticles**, are too big to leak out of healthy pipes. But they can slip through the cracks near the tumor. Tumors also have poor drains, so the bubbles get stuck there and stay. Scientists call this the **EPR effect**.

Scientists can also stick little "keys" onto the bubbles. The keys fit "locks" that cancer cells have on their outside. When a key finds its lock, the bubble grabs on and slips inside the cell. That is called **targeting**.
levels.hs:
Nanocarriers are particles roughly 10 to 200 nanometers across that carry drugs. Two strategies help them gather in diseased tissue.

**Passive targeting: the EPR effect.** EPR stands for **enhanced permeability and retention**. It was described in 1986 by Hiroshi Maeda and Yasuhiro Matsumura in Japan.
- **Enhanced permeability:** tumors grow new blood vessels quickly through a process called **angiogenesis**. These vessels are leaky, with gaps between their lining cells. Healthy vessels have tight junctions that keep large particles in.
- **Retention:** tumors have poor **lymphatic drainage**, so particles that leak out are not cleared quickly and build up.

Small drug molecules leak out of normal vessels everywhere, and they also wash out of tumors fast. Nanoparticles mostly stay in the blood until they reach a leaky spot.

**Active targeting.** Scientists attach **ligands** to the particle surface. Ligands are molecules that bind specific **receptors** found in larger numbers on diseased cells. Examples are antibodies, peptides, and small molecules like **folic acid**.

A real example: **Doxil**, a liposome version of the cancer drug doxorubicin, was approved in 1995 and relies on passive accumulation. It causes less heart damage than free doxorubicin. However, the EPR effect is much weaker and more variable in human tumors than in mouse tumors.
levels.college:
Nanomedicine targeting has two layers: getting particles to the tissue, and getting them into the right cells.

**The EPR effect (passive targeting)**
- Tumor vessels form through chaotic, VEGF-driven angiogenesis. They have discontinuous endothelium, fenestrations, and poor pericyte coverage. Gaps can range from roughly 100 nm to several hundred nm, depending on the tumor.
- Impaired lymphatics reduce clearance from the interstitium, so particles are retained.
- To use EPR, a particle needs a **long circulation time**. Each pass through the tumor is a chance to extravasate. Particles must also be large enough to avoid renal filtration (about 5.5 nm cutoff) but small enough to fit through the gaps. This sets a practical size window of about 10 to 200 nm.
- Inflamed tissue shows a related leakiness, sometimes called ELVIS (extravasation through leaky vasculature and inflammatory cell-mediated sequestration).

**Active targeting**
Ligands are conjugated to the particle surface, often at the distal ends of PEG chains, so they stay accessible.
- **Antibodies or fragments** (Fab, scFv), for example anti-HER2
- **Peptides**, for example cyclic **RGD**, which binds αvβ3 integrins on angiogenic endothelium
- **Aptamers**: folded nucleic acids
- **Small molecules**: folate (folate receptor-α), and PSMA ligands
- **Transferrin**, which binds transferrin receptor

A key point is often misunderstood. Active targeting mainly increases **cellular uptake** through receptor-mediated endocytosis and retention once particles are in the tissue. It does much less to increase total tumor accumulation, which still depends on extravasation. Ligand-bearing particles do not "home" from the bloodstream like guided missiles.

**Trade-offs:** ligands can speed clearance by the immune system. They also add manufacturing complexity, and the target receptor may also appear on healthy cells.
levels.phd:
Maeda's original 1986 work used the polymer conjugate SMANCS and protein tracers such as Evans blue-albumin. It showed that macromolecules above about 40 kDa accumulated selectively in murine tumors and persisted there. Later studies found that factors like bradykinin, nitric oxide, prostaglandins and VEGF worsen vascular leakiness.

**Quantitative reality.** Wilhelm and colleagues (Chan lab, Nature Reviews Materials 2016) did a meta-analysis of 117 papers. They found a median of about 0.7% of the injected dose reaching solid tumors. Active targeting improved this only modestly, from about 0.6% to 0.9%. Most of the dose goes to the liver and spleen through the mononuclear phagocyte system.

**Transport physics.** Extravasation is limited by **elevated interstitial fluid pressure** (IFP). Leaky vessels and absent lymphatics raise IFP to near-microvascular levels, which collapses the pressure gradient that drives convection. Delivery then relies on slow diffusion. Diffusion is hindered by dense collagen and hyaluronan, so large particles stay near the vessels. Cabral and Kataoka (2011) showed that 30 nm micelles penetrated poorly permeable pancreatic tumors, while 100 nm micelles did not.

**Challenging the gap paradigm.** Sindhwani and colleagues (Nature Materials 2020) used imaging and zombie-mouse models with chemically fixed vasculature. They reported that up to about 97% of nanoparticle entry occurs through **active transendothelial transport** (transcytosis), not through interendothelial gaps. This finding is contested, but it reframes EPR as partly an active, biologically regulated process.

**Active targeting nuances.**
- **Binding site barrier:** high-affinity ligands bind the first cells they meet near vessels, which limits deeper penetration.
- **Avidity:** multivalent display increases functional affinity. Optimal ligand density is non-monotonic, because too many ligands impair stealth and increase opsonization.
- **PEG shielding:** long PEG brushes can mask ligands. This is often addressed with longer PEG spacers for ligands.
- **Kirpotin et al. (2006):** anti-HER2 immunoliposomes did not raise total tumor accumulation compared with untargeted liposomes. They did markedly increase internalization into cancer cells and improve efficacy. This study is the classic demonstration of uptake rather than homing.
levels.expert:
Clinically, EPR remains the weak link in translating nanomedicines. Liposomal doxorubicin and nab-paclitaxel improved toxicity profiles rather than survival in most indications. Many targeted candidates have failed:
- **BIND-014**, a PSMA-targeted polymeric nanoparticle carrying docetaxel, showed modest phase 2 activity, and the company went bankrupt in 2016.
- **MM-302**, a HER2-targeted liposomal doxorubicin, stopped in phase 2 (HERMIONE) for futility.

The shared lesson is that a carrier designed for an "average" EPR fails in patients with low EPR.

**Patient stratification** is the major current strategy:
- **Ferumoxytol MRI:** Ramanathan and colleagues showed that ferumoxytol uptake correlated with lesion response to irinotecan liposome (MM-398, Onivyde).
- **PET companion imaging:** <sup>64</sup>Cu-labeled HER2-targeted liposomes used to grade deposition in patients.

Heterogeneity is huge. It varies between tumor types, between primary tumors and metastases, and even within a single lesion.

**Modulating EPR.** Approaches under study include:
- **Vascular normalization** with low-intensity anti-VEGF therapy (Jain's framework), which improves perfusion but may shrink pores
- **Losartan** to reduce collagen and lower solid stress
- **Nitroglycerin** and NO donors
- **Hyperthermia** and focused ultrasound with microbubbles
- **Tumor priming** with cytotoxic or radiation therapy

**Beyond tumors.** Two settings show real successes for targeting:
- **Liver hepatocytes:** GalNAc-siRNA conjugates such as givosiran and inclisiran bind the asialoglycoprotein receptor. They work without needing EPR because liver sinusoids are fenestrated.
- **Antibody-drug conjugates:** these show that ligand-receptor targeting works best when the construct is small enough to penetrate tissue.

**Pitfalls for researchers:**
- Subcutaneous xenografts in mice grow fast and are far leakier than human tumors.
- "Targeted" claims should be tested against **ligand-scrambled or isotype controls** matched for size and charge.
- Report %ID/g together with whole-body distribution.
- Receptor expression in cultured cells rarely reflects expression in vivo.

**For the brain**, the intact blood-brain barrier generally prevents EPR. Glioblastoma has a disrupted barrier in its enhancing core, but the infiltrative margin, the target that matters for neurosurgery, often has an intact barrier. **Open questions** include how transcytosis is regulated, how to build reliable biomarkers of EPR, and whether immune-cell hitchhiking can outperform passive delivery.

keyPoints: EPR = enhanced permeability (leaky tumor vessels) and retention (poor lymphatic drainage)
Long circulation and a size of about 10-200 nm let nanoparticles exploit EPR
Active targeting uses ligands (antibodies, peptides, folate, aptamers) that bind overexpressed receptors
Ligands mainly boost cell uptake, not total tumor accumulation
Median tumor delivery is only about 0.7% of the injected dose; EPR varies widely in humans
High interstitial pressure, dense stroma and the binding site barrier limit penetration

lessons.title: Protein Corona, Immune Clearance and Nanoparticle Fate

levels.kid: Picture a tiny delivery truck (a nanoparticle) carrying medicine through your blood. The moment it enters, sticky proteins from your blood glue themselves all over it, like mud splashing onto a bike. This sticky coat is called a "protein corona." Some of those proteins are like flags that call your body's cleanup crew — special cells in your liver and spleen that eat up anything that looks foreign. If too many flag-proteins stick, the truck gets eaten before it can deliver its medicine! Scientists give nanoparticles slippery, smooth coatings, kind of like a raincoat, so fewer proteins stick. That helps the truck slip past the cleanup crew and reach where it's needed, like a tumor.
levels.hs:
When a nanoparticle enters the bloodstream, proteins from blood plasma immediately stick to its surface, forming a layer called the **protein corona**. This corona becomes the nanoparticle's "biological identity" — what the immune system actually sees, rather than the original synthetic surface.

Some proteins act as **opsonins**: molecules like complement protein C3b and antibodies (IgG) that mark the particle for destruction. Immune cells called macrophages, concentrated in the liver (Kupffer cells) and spleen, recognize opsonin-coated particles and engulf them through a process called phagocytosis. This network of macrophages is called the **mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS)**. Other proteins, called **dysopsonins** (such as albumin), do the opposite — they help a particle blend in and avoid being eaten, extending how long it circulates.

Nanoparticle fate depends on this balance. Very small particles (under about 8 nanometers) can be filtered out by the kidneys and excreted in urine; larger ones are usually captured by the liver and spleen. A real example: PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil) uses a slippery polyethylene glycol coating to reduce opsonin binding, letting the drug circulate for days instead of minutes.
levels.college:
Within seconds of entering blood, a nanoparticle's surface is coated by plasma proteins, forming the **protein corona** — the layer that actually interfaces with cells and immune receptors, distinct from the particle's engineered "synthetic identity."

- **Hard vs. soft corona**: the hard corona consists of high-affinity proteins bound tightly with slow exchange (hours); the soft corona is a loosely associated, rapidly exchanging outer layer. Composition shifts over time through the **Vroman effect**, where abundant, high-mobility proteins (e.g., albumin) adsorb first but are gradually displaced by lower-abundance proteins with higher binding affinity (e.g., apolipoproteins, complement factors).
- **Opsonins vs. dysopsonins**: complement fragments (C3b, iC3b), IgG, and fibrinogen act as opsonins, recognized by complement receptors (CR3/CR4) and Fc receptors on phagocytes. Albumin, apolipoprotein A-I, and clusterin (apoJ) act as dysopsonins that suppress uptake and prolong circulation.
- **Mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS)**: Kupffer cells in liver sinusoids and marginal-zone macrophages in the spleen capture most opsonized nanoparticles within minutes to hours, making the liver and spleen the dominant off-target reservoirs for intravenously administered nanomedicines.
- **Renal clearance**: particles with hydrodynamic diameter below roughly 8 nm, and with neutral-to-cationic surface charge, pass through the glomerular filtration barrier and are excreted in urine; larger particles are cleared hepatobiliarly after MPS uptake and lysosomal processing.
- **Complement activation** can occur via the alternative, classical, or lectin pathways depending on surface chemistry (hydroxyl groups, charge, curvature), generating anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a that both promote clearance and can trigger acute hypersensitivity reactions.

Surface charge and PEGylation density strongly shape corona composition: cationic surfaces adsorb more opsonins and clear faster, while dense PEG brushes sterically reduce total protein adsorption, though they cannot eliminate corona formation entirely.
levels.phd:
The protein corona is now understood as a dynamic, patient-specific interface rather than a fixed coating. Proteomic studies (LC-MS/MS after differential centrifugation or magnetic/size-based separation) routinely identify 100-300 distinct plasma proteins on a single nanoparticle, with relative abundance governed by surface curvature, zeta potential, hydrophobicity, and PEG grafting density/conformation (mushroom vs. brush regime). Kenneth Dawson's group demonstrated that corona composition is reproducible enough under standardized conditions to generate particle-specific "fingerprints," while also showing that corona content varies measurably between individual donors and disease states (e.g., diabetic or cancer plasma), motivating proposals to use corona fingerprinting diagnostically.

Mechanistically, complement activation is central to clearance. Surface features favoring hydroxyl/amine exposure or certain curvatures trigger the alternative pathway via spontaneous C3 hydrolysis (C3(H2O)) and amplification through factors B and D, generating C3b/iC3b deposition recognized by CR3 (Mac-1, CD11b/CD18) on Kupffer cells and splenic macrophages. IgM/IgG-mediated classical pathway activation contributes when natural or induced antibodies bind the surface.

A key translational phenomenon is the **accelerated blood clearance (ABC) effect**, characterized extensively by Ishida, Kiwada and colleagues: a first dose of PEGylated liposomes elicits a T-cell-independent IgM response from splenic marginal-zone B cells directed against the PEG headgroup, peaking around day three to five. A second dose given in this window is rapidly opsonized by anti-PEG IgM, activates complement via the classical pathway, and is cleared from circulation within minutes rather than circulating for days — substantially undermining the pharmacokinetic rationale for PEGylation on repeat dosing.

A related acute phenomenon, **complement activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA)**, produces anaphylatoxin (C3a, C5a) surges that degranulate mast cells and basophils independent of IgE, explaining infusion reactions seen with some liposomal and micellar formulations within minutes of administration.

Controversy persists over how predictive in vitro corona profiling is of in vivo biodistribution, since static ex vivo incubation cannot fully capture shear flow, protein turnover, and cell-surface interactions present physiologically.
levels.expert:
Clinically, anti-PEG immunity has moved from a laboratory curiosity to a point-of-care concern. Serosurveys conducted before COVID-19 vaccination already found pre-existing anti-PEG IgG and/or IgM in a substantial fraction of the general population—often cited in the range of roughly a quarter to over half of donors depending on assay sensitivity—attributable to incidental PEG exposure in cosmetics, processed foods, and laxatives. This pre-existing immunity is now implicated in some of the rare but notable hypersensitivity reactions reported after PEGylated lipid-nanoparticle mRNA vaccines, prompting premedication protocols and renewed scrutiny of PEG as the default stealth polymer.

In response, delivery scientists are developing alternative stealth coatings that resist both opsonization and pre-existing adaptive immunity: zwitterionic polymers (polycarboxybetaine, polysulfobetaine), polysarcosine, and polyoxazolines provide comparably dense hydration shells without triggering, or being recognized by, anti-PEG antibodies, and are now in early clinical development for liposomal and lipid-nanoparticle platforms.

A second strategy borrows directly from self-recognition biology: nanoparticles can be cloaked in natural or synthetic "don't-eat-me" signals, most notably CD47-mimetic peptides or whole plasma-membrane coatings harvested from red blood cells, platelets, or leukocytes ("biomimetic" or "cell-membrane-cloaked" nanoparticles). These membrane coats present native CD47 and other self-markers to SIRPα on macrophages, measurably reducing MPS uptake in preclinical models and representing one of the more active areas of nanomedicine engineering today.

Open problems remain significant: corona composition measured ex vivo in bench assays correlates only imperfectly with in vivo macrophage uptake and biodistribution, complicating rational design; regulatory agencies lack standardized assays for predicting complement activation or ABC risk during preclinical development; and because corona composition is patient- and disease-specific, a formulation optimized in healthy-donor plasma may behave differently in an inflamed or hyperlipidemic patient. Predictive computational modeling of corona formation from first principles is an active but still immature research frontier.

keyPoints: Nanoparticles are rapidly coated by plasma proteins (protein corona) that define their biological identity
Opsonins (complement C3b, IgG) mark particles for immune destruction; dysopsonins (albumin, apoA-I) help particles evade clearance
The mononuclear phagocyte system (Kupffer cells, splenic macrophages) captures most IV nanoparticles via phagocytosis
Particles below roughly 8 nm are cleared renally; larger particles are cleared hepatobiliarly
Repeat dosing of PEGylated nanoparticles can trigger anti-PEG IgM and accelerated blood clearance (ABC phenomenon)
Complement activation can cause acute pseudoallergic infusion reactions (CARPA), independent of IgE

test.q: What is the protein corona?
choices: A synthetic polymer shell added during manufacturing
The metal core of a nanoparticle
A type of antibody used for targeting
A layer of plasma proteins that coats a nanoparticle's surface
test.explain: The protein corona forms when blood proteins adsorb onto a nanoparticle's surface, becoming its functional biological identity.

test.q: Which molecules act as opsonins by marking nanoparticles for immune destruction?
test.explain: C3b and IgG are classic opsonins recognized by complement receptors and Fc receptors on phagocytes; albumin and apoA-I are dysopsonins instead.

test.q: Which protein is described as a dysopsonin that helps nanoparticles evade clearance?
test.explain: Albumin suppresses phagocytic uptake and prolongs circulation, unlike fibrinogen, C5b-9, and IgM, which promote clearance.

test.q: Which two organs capture most intravenously injected nanoparticles through phagocytosis?
test.explain: Kupffer cells in the liver and marginal-zone macrophages in the spleen make up the bulk of the mononuclear phagocyte system that clears nanoparticles.

test.q: Nanoparticles below roughly what size can be cleared by the kidneys into urine?
test.explain: Particles with a hydrodynamic diameter below about 8 nm can pass through the glomerular filtration barrier; larger particles require liver or spleen clearance.

test.q: What is the main purpose of coating a nanoparticle with polyethylene glycol (PEG)?
choices: To add a fluorescent tag for imaging
To increase opsonin binding for faster clearance
To reduce protein adsorption and extend circulation time
test.explain: PEG forms a hydrated steric barrier that lowers total opsonin adsorption, letting particles like Doxil circulate longer.

test.q: The accelerated blood clearance (ABC) phenomenon occurs when:
choices: Anti-PEG IgM from the first dose opsonizes the second dose
Nanoparticles clump together due to increased blood viscosity levels
Dysopsonins bind more tightly to the particle surface afterward
Kidney filtration becomes faster after repeated dosing over time
test.explain: A first PEGylated dose triggers splenic anti-PEG IgM production, which opsonizes and rapidly clears a later dose via complement.

test.q: Complement activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA) causes infusion reactions through:
choices: IgE receptors on mast cells triggering allergic signaling directly
Anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a activating mast cells and basophils
Kidney cells releasing histamine into the bloodstream quickly
Toxic effects directly from the nanoparticle's core material
test.explain: CARPA is an IgE-independent reaction driven by complement anaphylatoxins triggering mast cell and basophil degranulation.

test.q: The Vroman effect describes how:
choices: Nanoparticles gradually shrink once inside the bloodstream environment
PEG chains quickly detach from the surface after one dose
Corona composition shifts over time as surface proteins exchange
Kidneys begin filtering nanoparticles much faster with repeated use
test.explain: High-mobility proteins adsorb first but are gradually replaced by lower-abundance, higher-affinity proteins, reshaping the corona over time.

test.q: What is the name of the immune cell network in the liver and spleen that captures most nanoparticles?
test.explain: The mononuclear phagocyte system includes Kupffer cells and splenic macrophages that engulf opsonized particles.

test.q: Large circulating proteins such as albumin that help nanoparticles avoid immune detection are called ___.
test.explain: Dysopsonins coat a particle without flagging it for phagocytosis, prolonging its time in circulation.

test.q: What is the brand name of a PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin formulation used as a real-world example of stealth nanoparticle design?
test.explain: Doxil's PEG coating reduces opsonin binding, giving it a much longer circulation time than unmodified liposomes.

kidTest.q: What sticks to a nanoparticle as soon as it enters the blood?
kidTest.explain: Blood proteins stick to the nanoparticle right away, forming its sticky coat.

kidTest.q: What do we call the immune cells that eat marked particles?
kidTest.explain: Macrophages are the cleanup cells that gobble up particles flagged by sticky proteins.

kidTest.q: Which two organs have lots of cleanup cells?
kidTest.explain: The liver and spleen are packed with macrophages that catch most nanoparticles.

kidTest.q: What slippery coating helps nanoparticles hide from the cleanup crew?
kidTest.explain: A PEG coating acts like a raincoat, helping fewer proteins stick so the particle can slip past the cleanup crew.

kidTest.q: What word describes the sticky protein coat on a nanoparticle? (hint: c _ _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: The sticky layer of proteins is called the protein corona.

advancedTest.q: Why does a second dose of PEGylated liposomes often get cleared much faster than the first dose (the ABC phenomenon)?
choices: PEG chains degrade between doses, exposing a more immunogenic lipid core
The first dose saturates kidney filtration, forcing liver clearance of the second dose
Repeated dosing increases nanoparticle size through aggregation in circulation
Splenic B cells produce anti-PEG IgM that opsonizes the second dose via complement
advancedTest.explain: The anti-PEG IgM response generated after the first dose opsonizes the second dose, activating complement and triggering rapid hepatic clearance.

advancedTest.q: Why might protein corona profiles measured in bench (in vitro) assays predict in vivo nanoparticle fate poorly?
choices: Static incubation misses the shear flow and protein turnover in blood
Nanoparticles carry a notably reduced surface charge outside the body
Plasma proteins tend to denature fairly quickly once outside the body
In vitro assays typically rely on a fixed protein concentration throughout
advancedTest.explain: Dynamic blood flow and ongoing protein exchange shape the corona in vivo in ways static bench incubations cannot replicate.

advancedTest.q: Pre-existing anti-PEG antibodies found in a substantial fraction of the general population are most plausibly explained by:
choices: Incidental PEG exposure from cosmetics, foods, and laxatives
Natural PEG production by human gut bacteria
Routine clinical use of PEGylated chemotherapy agents in most people
Universal neonatal vaccination schedules containing PEG
advancedTest.explain: Everyday incidental exposure to PEG in consumer products, not clinical PEGylated drugs, accounts for widespread pre-existing anti-PEG immunity.

advancedTest.q: Zwitterionic polymers and polysarcosine are being explored as PEG alternatives mainly because they:
choices: Increase nanoparticle size well above the typical renal filtration threshold
Provide a comparable hydration barrier while avoiding anti-PEG immunity
Remove the requirement for any protective surface coating on the nanoparticles
Bind opsonins more strongly to accelerate immune clearance of the particles
advancedTest.explain: These alternative coatings mimic PEG's steric, hydrated stealth effect while avoiding recognition by pre-existing anti-PEG antibodies.
